solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Detectives on Roman force thick and tenacious

indicators.note: in an across clue, a piece placed on another comes after it

parts.note: vis is the Latin word for force
CID = Criminal Investigation Department, the British police detectives

explanation.surface: A police procedural set in ancient Rome, with detectives joining a tough, dogged legion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Roman force' suggests a legion or the Roman police; it wants the Latin word for force itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Viscid describes something sticky and glutinous, so thick and tenacious in the way treacle clings.

clue.text: Tiny hole in tank terminal for that old canal boat

indicators.note: the tiny hole sits inside the tank

parts.note: a vat is a large tank, here split VA…T around the hole
a pore is a tiny opening in the skin

indicators.note: the terminal of a word is its final letter

parts.note: the last letter of thaT
O = old, a standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: A leaky old narrowboat whose water tank has sprung a tiny hole.
explanation.walkthrough: The canal in question is Venetian: a vaporetto is the water-bus of Venice. Note 'that old' is not a phrase; T comes from 'that' and O from 'old'.
explanation.definitionFit: A vaporetto is the motor boat that serves as public transport on the canals of Venice.

clue.text: Venerable Hindu perhaps crawled over India

parts.note: the crawl is a swimming stroke, so to have crawled is to have swum
India is I in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: An aged holy man inching his way across India on hands and knees.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crawled' pictures creeping on all fours; it is the swimming stroke. 'Over' in a down clue simply puts SWAM on top of I.
explanation.definitionFit: Swami is a title of respect for a Hindu religious teacher, so a venerable Hindu, 'perhaps' because not every such person is one.

clue.text: Wonky line cut by fine horse unsuited to ploughing

indicators.note: wonky means crooked, so the letters of LINE go askew
the horse cuts into the rearranged line, splitting it in two

parts.note: LINE rearranged, then split IN…LE
the Arab is a prized breed of horse

explanation.surface: A crooked furrow ruined by a thoroughbred that was never meant to pull a plough.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fine' is just praise for the horse, not a separate instruction; the Arab is a noble breed, which is why it is no plough horse.
explanation.definitionFit: Arable land can be ploughed and farmed, so inarable land is unsuited to ploughing.

clue.text: Spotted smoked ham was in the van

parts.note: speck is a smoked ham from the Tyrol
to be in the van (vanguard) is to be at the front, leading

explanation.surface: A deli delivery: someone saw a smoked ham riding in the delivery van.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spotted' looks like the verb 'saw' opening a sighting; it is the adjective. 'The van' is the vanguard, not a vehicle.
explanation.definitionFit: Speckled means marked with small spots.

clue.text: Sit around drunk at four, late out of theatre

parts.note: to sit for a portrait is to pose; split POS…E
a toper is a heavy drinker
used as it stands
Roman numeral four

explanation.surface: A drinker still propping up the bar at four, far too late to leave the theatre.
explanation.walkthrough: The theatre is an operating theatre, not a playhouse; 'late out of' means lately out of, just after surgery.
explanation.definitionFit: Post-operative describes the period just after an operation, when a patient is newly out of the operating theatre.

clue.text: Conservative begins Hard Times

parts.note: C = Conservative, the British party
rises = begins, as a river or a day does

explanation.surface: A Tory reading Dickens: a Conservative starts on Hard Times.
explanation.walkthrough: The capitals make 'Hard Times' the Dickens novel; the definition wants the plain words, times of hardship.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym once the capitals are ignored: a crisis is a spell of acute difficulty or danger.

clue.text: Fancy something strong to drink quickly

parts.note: to fancy something is to like it
a shot is a small measure of spirits

explanation.surface: Someone at the bar tempted to knock back a stiff drink in one go.
explanation.walkthrough: The drinking picture sets up 'quickly' as how the drink goes down, but it is the definition on its own.
explanation.definitionFit: To do something like a shot is to do it instantly and eagerly.

clue.text: Divine young woman in towel commercial

parts.note: to towel something is to dry it
an ad is a commercial

explanation.surface: A gorgeous model in a TV advert for towels.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Divine' reads as 'gorgeous' and describes the model; it means literally divine, a minor goddess.
explanation.definitionFit: A dryad is a tree nymph of Greek myth, a young female spirit of divine nature.

clue.text: Notice young man secures vehicle after parking

indicators.note: the young man holds the vehicle inside him

parts.note: P = parking, as on road signs
a lad is a young man; split LA…D
a car is a vehicle

explanation.surface: A notice that a young man locks up his car after parking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After parking' puts P first even though it comes last in the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: A placard is a sign or poster displayed as a public notice.

clue.text: Panic spread beginning in economy, a turbulent flight?

indicators.note: turbulent means churned up, so the letters are mixed

parts.note: anagram fodder

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its first letter

parts.note: the first letter of Economy
used as it stands, the last of the fodder

explanation.surface: A nervous passenger in economy class panicking on a bumpy flight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flight' is set up as a plane journey by 'economy' and 'turbulent'; it means running away. The question mark flags that twist.
explanation.definitionFit: Flight is fleeing, and fleeing makes someone vanish: a disappearance.

clue.text: Last of runners flash past — don't give up

indicators.note: take only the final letter

parts.note: the last letter of runnerS
a tick and a flash both mean an instant
to go past is to go by

explanation.surface: Encouragement to the tail-ender in a race as the leaders flash past.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flash' looks like a verb of speed next to 'runners'; it is the noun, a moment, as in 'back in a tick'.
explanation.definitionFit: To stick by someone is to stay loyal and not give up on them.

clue.text: Indian side cheers on attack that lacks depth

indicators.note: to lack something is to be without it, and depth abbreviates to D, so RAID loses its D
in an across clue, 'on' puts the first piece after the second

parts.note: RAID without D (depth)
ta is British slang for thanks, and cheers means thanks

explanation.surface: A cricket report: the Indian team cheers an attack lacking depth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Indian side' sounds like a cricket team; it is a side dish. Raita is the yogurt and cucumber accompaniment to a curry.
explanation.definitionFit: Raita is a yogurt dish served on the side with Indian food.

clue.text: Cannonball shortly due to land

indicators.note: the word is cut short by its last letter

parts.note: SHOT, a cannonball, cut short
one's due is what one deserves, a reward

explanation.surface: A cannonball about to come down on land any moment now.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shortly due' looks like 'expected soon'; 'shortly' belongs to the cannonball, and 'due' is a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Shoreward means towards the shore, in the direction of land.

clue.text: Ship leaves once loaded

parts.note: the surface reading: a ship departs; the meant reading: a ship's cargo of (tea) leaves
the surface reading: as soon as it is loaded; the meant reading: formerly laden, with that cargo

explanation.surface: A ship setting sail as soon as its cargo is aboard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leaves' reads as the verb 'departs'; it is the noun, tea leaves, which the ship once carried as cargo. 'Once' points to its nineteenth-century heyday.
explanation.definitionFit: A tea clipper was a fast sailing ship that carried tea from China to Britain in the nineteenth century.

clue.text: A bit of skin cook sliced off sounds attractive

indicators.note: it is the sound of the phrase that gives the answer

parts.words: A bit of skin cook sliced off
parts.note: a peeling is a strip of skin pared off a vegetable

explanation.surface: A cook who has sliced off a bit of their finger, not an attractive sight.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a kitchen injury; the skin is a vegetable's, and 'a peeling' said aloud is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: something appealing draws you towards it.

clue.text: High street business, can it work?

parts.note: 'can it!' means 'be quiet!', which is sh
op = opus, a work

explanation.surface: A worried owner wondering whether a high street business can be made to pay.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Can it work?' reads as a question about viability; 'can it' is slang for shut up. A high street is a town's main shopping street.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: retail premises are the typical high street business, alongside banks and cafés.

clue.text: Sphinxlike features Oscar saw cut in step

parts.note: a pace is a step; split P…ACE
Oscar is O in the NATO phonetic alphabet
a kerf is the slit made by a saw

explanation.surface: Oscar watching an enigmatic statue being sawn apart in step, face giving nothing away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Saw' looks like the past of 'see', with Oscar watching; it is the tool, and the cut it makes has its own name, kerf.
explanation.definitionFit: The Sphinx is famously inscrutable, and a poker face is an expression that gives nothing away.

clue.text: Round of applause a little generous

parts.note: to give someone a hand is to applaud them
some = a little

explanation.surface: An audience grudging with its applause, which was only a little generous.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Handsome' is used here in its sense of ample, as in a handsome tip, not good-looking.
explanation.definitionFit: An older sense of the word: a handsome tip or offer is liberal in amount, nothing to do with looks.

clue.text: Only two-thirds of cutlery put back, oh dear

indicators.note: keep four of the six letters
put back means turned round

parts.note: SPOONS, a kind of cutlery, trimmed to its first four of six letters

explanation.surface: Someone clearing up finds only two-thirds of the cutlery was returned to the drawer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cutlery' has to become a specific six-letter item before two-thirds of it can be taken; SPOONS gives SPOO.
explanation.definitionFit: Oops is the exclamation of someone who has just made a small blunder, like oh dear.

clue.text: 20C composer's babel developed technique, all right

indicators.note: the letters of babel are worked into a new shape

parts.note: anagram fodder
an art is a skill or technique
OK = all right

explanation.surface: A critic grudgingly admitting that a modern composer's din has a sound technique.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Babel' reads as a racket of discordant music; it is only letters. 20C is the twentieth century.
explanation.definitionFit: Béla Bartók was a Hungarian composer of the twentieth century.

clue.text: Monster logically following that capsized ship

indicators.note: a capsized boat is upside down, so in a down clue the word is turned over

parts.note: ergo = therefore, what logically follows
SS = steamship

explanation.surface: A monster following a ship that has overturned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capsized' seems to belong to the ship; it acts on ERGO. The definition is looser than the answer, since an ogress is a female ogre.
explanation.definitionFit: An ogress is a female ogre, a man-eating monster of folklore.

clue.text: NZ city with large aviation facility that is in recession

parts.note: w = with, as in w/
a hangar houses aircraft

indicators.note: receding means going backwards, so the letters run in reverse

parts.note: i.e. = that is

explanation.surface: A New Zealand city with a big airport hangar at a time of economic downturn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In recession' looks like economic news; it turns IE round. Whangarei is a city in the far north of New Zealand's North Island.
explanation.definitionFit: Whangarei is a city in Northland, New Zealand.

clue.text: What rambler does having lost new waterproof boot

parts.note: a rambler wanders
N = new, removed from WANDER

explanation.surface: A hiker who has lost a new waterproof boot.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a hiker's mishap; 'having lost new' is the instruction to drop N from WANDER.
explanation.definitionFit: A wader is a high waterproof boot worn for standing in water.

clue.text: Celebration instead of defeat

parts.note: a do is a party
as in 'swap this for that'

explanation.surface: A party held in place of a loss.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface sets celebration against defeat as opposites; 'defeat' is the definition, and 'do for' is informal for finish off.
explanation.definitionFit: To do for someone is to ruin or finish them off, to defeat them.

clue.text: Female dressing, a stone lighter

parts.note: F = female
lint is a soft fabric used to dress wounds

explanation.surface: A woman in a wound dressing, now a stone lighter after dieting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A stone lighter' reads as weight lost; it is a stone that lights, the flint struck to make a spark.
explanation.definitionFit: Flint is a hard stone that sparks when struck, used as the lighter in cigarette lighters.

clue.text: Blood vessel opened by doctor, one showing concern for the motorist

parts.note: Dr = doctor
I = one, the Roman numeral
a vein is a blood vessel

explanation.surface: A doctor opening a vein, a caring medic attending a motorist after a crash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Showing' and 'concern' suggest care; a drive-in is a business, especially a cinema, showing films to people in their cars.
explanation.definitionFit: A drive-in cinema is one showing films to motorists, a concern (business) for them.

clue.text: Adult works at aerobics, desperately wanting shaped abs

indicators.note: done desperately, the letters are thrown about
wanting means lacking, so ABS is removed

parts.note: used as it stands, part of the fodder
AEROBICS without the letters A, B, S

explanation.surface: An adult working out at aerobics, desperate for a sculpted six-pack.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Adult works' passes for a grown-up who exercises; it is adult material. 'Shaped' makes the removed letters form ABS in any order.
explanation.definitionFit: Erotica are literary or artistic works of a sexual nature, adult works.

clue.text: Roll touching substance that's dubious

parts.note: re = regarding, touching on
the gist is the substance of a matter
er is the hesitant noise of someone unsure

explanation.surface: A bread roll that has been handled by some questionable stuff.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Roll' reads as bread; it is a roll of names, as in a roll call.
explanation.definitionFit: A roll is an official list of names, a register.

clue.text: Little Scottish collars its, on reflection?

definitions.text: Little Scottish collars its, on reflection?

indicators.note: a reflection is reversed, so ITS turns round

parts.note: wee is Scots for little; split WE…E
ITS reversed

explanation.surface: A small Scottish dog regarding its own collar in a mirror.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is also the definition: a westie is a little Scottish dog, and dogs wear collars. The question mark flags that double duty.
explanation.definitionFit: A westie is a West Highland white terrier, a small Scottish breed that wears a collar like any dog.
